In this talk we briefly summarize our theoretical understanding of in-medium selfenergies of hadrons. With the special case of the $\omega$ meson we demonstrate that earlier calculations that predicted a significant lowering of the mass in medium are based on an incorrect treatment of the model Lagrangian; more consistent calculations lead to a significant broadening, but hardly any mass shift. We stress that the experimental reconstruction of hadron spectral functions from measured decay products always requires knowledge of the decay branching ratios which may also be strongly mass-dependent. It also requires a quantitatively reliable treatment of final state interactions which has to be part of any reliable theory.

outputs.L1: In this talk, we briefly summarize our theoretical understanding of the in-medium self-energies of hadrons. Using the $\omega$ meson as a specific example, we demonstrate that earlier calculations predicting a significant reduction in its in-medium mass were based on an incorrect treatment of the model Lagrangian. More consistent calculations instead indicate substantial broadening, with hardly any mass shift. We emphasize that experimentally reconstructing hadron spectral functions from measured decay products invariably requires knowledge of the relevant decay branching ratios, which may themselves depend strongly on mass. Such reconstruction also requires a quantitatively reliable treatment of final-state interactions, which must be an integral part of any robust theoretical framework.
outputs.L2: This presentation offers a concise overview of the theoretical picture of hadron self-energies in a medium. Using the \(\omega\) meson as an example, we show that previous studies forecasting a substantial in-medium mass reduction relied on an improper handling of the model Lagrangian. More consistent approaches instead indicate pronounced broadening with almost no change in mass. We emphasize that extracting hadronic spectral functions experimentally from observed decay products depends on knowing the relevant decay branching fractions, which themselves can vary strongly with mass. In addition, any dependable theoretical framework must include a quantitatively accurate description of final-state interactions.
outputs.L3:
The talk reviews the theoretical understanding of hadron self-energies in a nuclear medium, with particular emphasis on the modification of meson properties. Earlier studies predicted a significant in-medium reduction of the \(\omega\)-meson mass. However, this result was subsequently traced to an inconsistent treatment of the underlying model Lagrangian and is therefore not considered reliable.

More consistent theoretical calculations indicate a different behavior: the \(\omega\) meson is expected to undergo substantial broadening in the medium, while its mass shifts only slightly. Thus, the dominant in-medium effect is an increase in the width of its spectral function rather than a pronounced displacement of the spectral peak.

Connecting these theoretical predictions to experimental measurements presents additional challenges. Hadron spectral functions are typically reconstructed from observed decay products, so the analysis depends on the relevant decay branching ratios. Because these branching ratios may themselves vary with the invariant mass and the surrounding medium, treating them as constants can distort the inferred spectral distribution. Moreover, the decay products may undergo rescattering, absorption, or other final-state interactions before reaching the detector. Reliable theoretical interpretations must therefore include a quantitative treatment of these effects in order to distinguish genuine in-medium modifications from distortions caused by the decay and propagation processes.
outputs.L4:
The talk reviews theoretical approaches to calculating hadron self-energies in nuclear matter, with particular emphasis on how such calculations are connected to experimentally reconstructed spectral functions. The ω meson serves as a representative case because its in-medium properties have been studied using a variety of effective model Lagrangians and have often been interpreted as possible evidence for changes in hadron masses inside nuclei.

A central issue is the reliability and internal consistency of the theoretical treatment. Earlier model calculations predicted a sizable downward shift of the ω-meson mass in nuclear matter. A careful reassessment shows, however, that these conclusions can depend strongly on approximations, coupling choices, and the treatment of intermediate states. When all relevant contributions to the ω self-energy are handled consistently, the dominant medium effect is a substantial increase in the meson’s width. In contrast, the position of the spectral peak—and therefore the effective ω mass—changes very little.

The discussion also stresses that the in-medium spectral function cannot be inferred directly from a measured invariant-mass distribution. Experiments observe particular decay channels, and the probability for an ω meson to appear in a given channel depends on mass-dependent partial widths and branching ratios. Treating branching fractions as constants can therefore distort the reconstructed line shape and may create an apparent mass shift that is not present in the underlying spectral function.

Final-state interactions provide an additional complication. After the ω decays inside the nucleus, its decay products may scatter, be absorbed, or lose energy before reaching the detector. These processes can redistribute events in invariant mass and alter both the shape and normalization of the measured spectrum. A realistic comparison between theory and experiment must consequently combine the in-medium ω self-energy with a consistent description of decay kinematics, mass-dependent branching ratios, nuclear geometry, particle propagation, and detector acceptance.

The resulting picture differs markedly from earlier claims of a pronounced in-medium mass reduction. Consistent calculations support strong collisional broadening of the ω meson but yield almost no shift of its mass. This conclusion highlights the danger of identifying modifications of an observed decay spectrum directly with changes in a hadron’s intrinsic mass. Reliable extraction of in-medium properties requires control over the full reaction and decay process, especially the branching behavior of an off-shell meson and the final-state interactions of its decay products.
outputs.L5:
### Understanding the Lagrangian

With the **Lagrangian** formulation, many problems in physics can be described elegantly through energy rather than forces. The Lagrangian is usually defined as

\[
L = T - V,
\]

where \(T\) is the kinetic energy of a system and \(V\) is its potential energy.

A physical system follows the path that makes the action

\[
S = \int L\,dt
\]

stationary. This principle leads to the Euler–Lagrange equation:

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q}\right)
-
\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=0.
\]

Here, \(q\) represents a generalized coordinate and \(\dot q\) its time derivative. Unlike Newtonian mechanics, which works directly with forces, Lagrangian mechanics can handle complicated coordinates and constraints naturally. It is therefore central not only to classical mechanics but also to electromagnetism, quantum field theory, and modern particle physics.

counterfactuals.output: We present a theoretical study of in-medium hadron self-energies, with emphasis on the \(\omega\) meson in nuclear matter. The real and imaginary parts of the self-energy generate density- and momentum-dependent mass shifts and spectral broadening, modifying the \(\omega\) spectral function and its observable decay patterns. We discuss how competing decay channels and in-medium branching ratios affect dilepton and hadronic signals. Particular attention is given to final-state interactions, including absorption, rescattering, and regeneration of decay products, which can obscure genuine medium modifications. The results highlight the need for a consistent treatment of production, propagation, decay, and transport when extracting in-medium hadron properties from nuclear experiments.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize current theoretical understanding of hadron spectral functions in nuclear matter and explain why earlier predictions of a large in-medium $\omega$-meson mass reduction may be incorrect.
counterfactuals.output:
In nuclear matter, a hadron is no longer characterized by a single sharply shifted mass. The relevant object is its spectral function  
\[
A_h(\omega,\mathbf q;\rho)=-\frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathrm{Im}\,D_h(\omega,\mathbf q;\rho),
\]
which reflects both the real and imaginary parts of the in-medium self-energy.

### Present theoretical picture

Hadronic many-body calculations, effective field theory, coupled-channel approaches, and QCD sum rules broadly suggest:

- **Collisional broadening is generally more robust than a large mass shift.** Scattering, absorption, resonance-hole excitations, and modified decay channels spread spectral strength over a wide energy range.
- **Spectral functions can become asymmetric or multi-peaked.** A quoted “mass” may refer to the propagator pole, the maximum of the spectrum, or a moment of the distribution; these need not move in the same way.
- **Vector mesons behave differently.** The \(\rho\) is expected to broaden strongly through modified pion dynamics and baryon-resonance excitations, usually with only a modest shift of its main strength. The vacuum-narrow \(\omega\) also acquires a substantial collision width through processes such as \(\omega N\to \pi N,\pi\pi N\) and resonance-hole coupling.
- At normal nuclear density, many calculations obtain an \(\omega\) width of roughly several tens to around \(100\) MeV, depending on momentum and model. Its pole or peak shift is much less settled: modest attraction, nearly no shift, and small repulsive shifts all occur. A universal \(15\!-\!20\%\) downward mass shift is not regarded as a robust prediction.
- Finite momentum additionally separates longitudinal and transverse modes, so there is not necessarily one unique in-medium spectral function.

### Why early large \(\omega\)-mass drops may be misleading

Early QCD sum-rule and scaling analyses often represented the spectrum by a narrow pole plus a perturbative continuum. Changes in the sum-rule moments were then necessarily interpreted as a movement of that pole. Several issues weaken that conclusion:

1. **QCD sum rules constrain moments, not a unique peak mass.** The same moment changes can be produced by broadening, low-energy strength, a shifted continuum threshold, or a multi-component spectrum without a large pole shift.

2. **The narrow-pole approximation becomes poor in matter.** Once the \(\omega\) develops a sizable collision width, fitting it with a zero-width pole can artificially turn broadening and redistribution into an apparent mass decrease.

3. **The density dependence of four-quark condensates is poorly known.** These condensates strongly influence vector-meson sum rules. Early work commonly used vacuum-saturation or simple factorization assumptions, which are not controlled at finite density and can bias the extracted shift downward.

4. **Nucleon-scattering, or Landau-damping, terms are important.** The vector current can scatter directly from nucleons, producing low-energy spectral strength. This contribution is especially important in the isoscalar \(\omega\) channel because of its stronger coupling to nucleon number. Omitting or underestimating it tends to exaggerate a downward mass shift; when treated consistently, it can offset the decrease or even favor an upward moment shift.

5. **Continuum and operator-product-expansion uncertainties were often restricted too strongly.** Fixing the continuum threshold, truncating the OPE, and using the linear-density approximation can make the extracted pole mass appear much more definite than it is.

6. **A simple link to the chiral condensate is not justified.** Partial restoration of chiral symmetry does not require every hadron mass to scale directly with \(\langle\bar q q\rangle\). Chiral restoration constrains relations between chiral-partner spectral functions and integrated strength, not necessarily a universal dropping-mass law.

Thus, the more defensible modern conclusion is that nuclear matter causes substantial restructuring and broadening of hadronic spectral functions. For the \(\omega\), a large downward mass shift is possible only under particular assumptions about condensates and \(\omega N\) dynamics; it is not a model-independent consequence of QCD or chiral restoration.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
**Broadening Without a Large Mass Shift: The In-Medium \(\omega\) Meson and Its Experimental Reconstruction**

We present a consistent treatment of the model Lagrangian for the \(\omega\) meson in nuclear matter, applying the same interaction vertices and approximations to both the real and imaginary parts of its self-energy. The resulting in-medium spectral function exhibits substantial collisional broadening, driven by scattering and resonance–hole excitations, while the net displacement of the spectral strength—and hence the apparent mass shift—remains comparatively small. This outcome highlights why mass shifts inferred from selected diagrams or incomplete treatments of the self-energy can be misleading: contributions to the dispersive part tend to cancel, even as available in-medium reaction channels significantly increase the width.

We then discuss why establishing this pattern experimentally is difficult. The observed line shape is distorted by nuclear density averaging, finite detector acceptance and resolution, final-state interactions, combinatorial backgrounds, and the large fraction of \(\omega\) mesons that decay outside the dense region. Hadronic decay modes offer statistics but suffer strong rescattering, whereas dilepton channels provide cleaner access to the spectral function at the cost of low branching ratios and substantial backgrounds. The talk will emphasize reconstruction strategies and observables capable of separating genuine in-medium broadening from kinematic and instrumental effects, and will clarify what current measurements can—and cannot—say about an \(\omega\)-mass shift.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a short technical paragraph about in-medium modifications of hadrons, including the mass dependence of decay branching ratios and the need for reliable modeling of final-state interactions.
counterfactuals.output: In nuclear matter, hadrons can acquire modified masses and widths through interactions with the surrounding medium, altering their spectral functions and decay patterns. Because partial decay widths depend on the available phase space and thus on the in-medium hadron mass, branching ratios may differ substantially from their vacuum values, especially near kinematic thresholds. Extracting these modifications from experimental observables therefore requires reliable modeling of final-state interactions, including rescattering, absorption, and charge exchange of the decay products as they propagate through the medium.

counterfactuals.output:
### In-Medium Selfenergies of Hadrons

The extraction of hadron properties in nuclear matter requires a consistent connection between in-medium selfenergies, spectral functions, and experimentally observed decay products. We critically reassess earlier calculations of the ω-meson selfenergy, emphasizing limitations arising from incomplete resonance contributions, oversimplified low-density approximations, insufficient treatment of coupled channels and medium modifications, and inconsistencies between production, propagation, and decay. Predictions of mass shifts or collision broadening alone cannot be directly identified with measured invariant-mass distributions. A reliable determination of the ω and other hadron spectral functions requires realistic nuclear geometry, momentum-dependent selfenergies, off-shell transport, and a coherent treatment of competing decay modes. Equally important are final-state interactions, absorption, rescattering, and regeneration of the decay products, together with detector acceptance, kinematic cuts, and experimental resolution. Only by embedding a theoretically constrained spectral function in a complete reaction model—and validating that model against elementary and nuclear reference data—can observed line shapes be interpreted as evidence for genuine in-medium modifications of hadrons.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
